title: 27 A preliminary study: Investigating the impacts of semen collection method on semen quality and physiological parameters in Boer goats
content:
Abstract
In the small ruminant industry, semen collected from top sires has several applications such as artificial insemination, breeding soundness exams, and storage through cryopreservation. The two most utilized semen collection methods are electroejaculation (EE) and artificial vagina (AV). However, previous research has indicated that EE poses an animal welfare concern and has shown negative impacts on sperm quality and concentration. The objective of this preliminary study was to evaluate the impact of semen collection method (AV vs EE) on semen quality and physiological parameters in Boer goats. Seven (n = 7) mature Boer bucks from a single source were utilized for semen collection during the breeding season (late October). Prior to semen collection, baseline physiological measurements, including FAMACHA score, heart rate, scrotal circumference, and rectal temperature were collected. Prior to semen collection, bucks were trained to be collected using the AV and an estrous doe. Semen collection for both techniques occurred on the same day, with all bucks first being collected using the AV. To ensure bucks had an adequate rest period, semen was collected via EE 3 hours post collection with the AV. Semen was diluted with a commercially-available extender (1:10) prior to evaluation. Semen volume, pH, concentration, and motility were evaluated immediately following collection. Sperm motility and concentration were determined utilizing a mobile computer assisted sperm analysis (CASA) system (AndroScope, Minitube USA, Inc., Verona, WI). Sperm morphology was conducted later utilizing a microscope with CASA (AndroVision, Minitube USA, Inc., Verona, WI) after staining samples with SpermBlue (Microtic S.L., Barcelona, Spain). To evaluate the impact of semen collection technique on physiological status, heart rate was collected at 5, 10, and 15 minutes post semen collection. Semen and physiological measures were analyzed using analysis of variance in JMP Pro v. 17.0. Heart rate was 12% greater following collection using EE compared to collection using AV (P = 0.02). Rectal temperature was not impacted by semen collection technique (P = 0.77). Semen volume and motility were greater (P ≤ 0.05) for samples collected using AV as compared to EE (1.6 vs 0.7 mL; 85.6 vs 70.3%, respectively). Additionally, semen concentration was greater (P ≤ 0.05) for samples collected using AV compared to EE (160.7 vs. 91.3 x 106, respectively). The percentage of intact sperm, sperm with abnormal heads, and sperm classified as having fast motility were not impacted by collection method (P ≥ 0.26). Semen collected utilizing the AV showed advantages in terms of semen quality as well as promoting the positive animal welfare of Boer goats. This preliminary study indicates the need for further research investigating the impacts of semen collection technique on semen quality and animal welfare in small ruminants.
